title: Extra Charge for Breakroom Deep Sanitization? How to Tell What Your Base Retainer Already Covers
seoTitle: Extra Charge Breakroom Deep Sanitization: Included vs Add-On Audit
metaDescription: Extra charge breakroom deep sanitization explained: $12–$25 per visit add-on vs folded-in retainer scope. Audit your contract, then compare quotes line by line.
excerpt: Most janitorial retainers cover a daily breakroom wipe-down but bill appliance interiors, fridge purges, and degreasing as separate work orders. This audit guide shows US office managers exactly where the line usually falls and how to negotiate it into the base price.
quickAnswer: Daily breakroom sanitation (counters, sink, microwave, fridge exterior, cabinet pulls) is usually either folded into the base rate or billed as a $12–$25 per-visit add-on, which works out to roughly $260–$540 per month on a five-day schedule. True deep sanitization (refrigerator purge, oven or toaster-oven degreasing, ice machine and coffee brewer descaling, behind-appliance floor work) is almost always a separate work order priced at $55–$95 per specialty labor hour with a $90–$135 minimum. Read the scope exhibit, not the sales proposal, to see which category your vendor is pricing.

blocks.text: Why the breakroom is the most disputed line in office cleaning contracts

Ask ten janitorial vendors whether the breakroom is included and you will get ten versions of yes. The problem is that yes usually means a crew member wipes the counters, empties the trash, and runs a damp cloth over the microwave door. It rarely means pulling every container out of the refrigerator, degreasing the toaster oven, or descaling the coffee brewer. When the office manager discovers a moldy produce drawer in month four and asks for it to be handled, the vendor issues a project invoice, and the dispute begins.

The fix is not a better relationship with the account manager. It is a scope exhibit that separates routine breakroom sanitation from periodic deep sanitization, assigns a frequency to each task, and states whether each line is in the base price or billed on a work order. This guide walks through how vendors typically draw that line, what each side of it costs, and how to audit an existing agreement.
Routine sanitation vs deep sanitization: where vendors draw the line

Industry pricing models treat breakroom sanitation as a per-visit add-on of roughly $12 to $25, covering countertops, the sink basin and faucet, microwave interior and exterior, refrigerator exterior and handle, and high-touch cabinet pulls. Some vendors fold that cost into the per-square-foot base rate and list it as included; others break it out. Either is fine as long as the tasks are written down. Deep sanitization tasks sit outside that per-visit envelope because they require emptying appliances, longer chemical dwell times, and sometimes moving equipment.

blocks.title: Monthly math on the per-visit add-on
blocks.text: A $12–$25 breakroom add-on on a five-day schedule (21.65 visits per month using 4.33 weeks) equals about $260–$541 per month. On a three-day schedule (13 visits) it is $156–$325. If a vendor quotes a flat breakroom line well above those figures, ask which deep tasks are bundled in; if it is well below, assume deep tasks are excluded.
Contract language that signals an extra charge is coming

Vendors rarely hide exclusions on purpose, but standard proposals use soft language that leaves room for project billing. Watch for the following phrasing in the scope or the exclusions page, because each one usually converts into a separate invoice the first time you ask for the work.

items: "Clean breakroom surfaces" with no appliance list: interiors are probably excluded.
"Appliance interiors upon request": request equals work order, typically billed at the specialty hourly rate.
"Client responsible for refrigerator contents": the crew will not discard food, so a purge requires your staff to clear it or a scheduled cleanout day.
"Periodic tasks quoted separately": everything beyond daily wiping is outside the retainer.
"Excludes kitchen equipment": coffee brewers, ice machines, and dishwashers are not touched at all.
No frequency column: without one, the vendor decides how often deep tasks happen, which usually means never unless prompted.

blocks.text: When folding deep sanitization into the retainer makes financial sense

Bundling makes sense when deep tasks are predictable. If you know the refrigerator gets purged every Friday and the brewer gets descaled monthly, the vendor can schedule labor, and you can negotiate a flat monthly figure instead of paying the $90–$135 minimum each time a work order is opened. For a 40-person office with one breakroom, one refrigerator, one brewer, and one microwave, a weekly purge plus monthly descale typically adds 1.5 to 2.5 crew hours per month. At $35–$65 standard hourly labor folded into the retainer, that is roughly $55–$165 per month, versus four separate purge work orders that could each hit the minimum.

Separate work orders make more sense when the need is irregular: a seasonal kitchen refresh before a client event, a one-time cleanout after a lease takeover, or a pest-response sanitization. In those cases, paying the specialty rate of $55–$95 per hour for a defined event is cheaper than carrying the cost every month.

blocks.text: How to audit your current agreement in one afternoon

items.name: Pull the signed scope exhibit
items.text: Ignore the glossy proposal. Find the task-frequency matrix attached to the signed agreement and locate every line mentioning breakroom, kitchenette, pantry, or appliances.

items.name: List every appliance you own
items.text: Count refrigerators, microwaves, toaster ovens, brewers, ice machines, and dishwashers. Each should appear in the scope with an interior and exterior frequency, or explicitly in the exclusions.

items.name: Review twelve months of invoices
items.text: Total every work order touching the breakroom. If ad-hoc charges exceed about $150 per month on average, bundling deep tasks into the retainer is likely cheaper.

items.name: Confirm chemical and safety documentation
items.text: Ask for Safety Data Sheets for degreasers and descalers under OSHA HazCom, and confirm food-contact surfaces receive a food-safe sanitizer or a potable-water rinse after disinfectant dwell time.

items.name: Rewrite the line items
items.text: Request a revised exhibit with each deep task, its frequency, and a fixed monthly price or a fixed per-event price that does not trigger the minimum charge.

blocks.title: Food disposal and liability
blocks.text: Crews are often instructed never to discard employee food. If your scope calls for a weekly refrigerator purge, publish an internal rule such as everything unlabeled is discarded Friday at 3 p.m., and give the vendor written authorization. Without it, the crew may skip the purge and still bill the visit.
Supplies and equipment that change the breakroom line item

Consumables affect how vendors price breakroom work. If the vendor supplies liners and towels, expect the consumables line of about $0.012–$0.025 per sq ft per visit. Heavy wet waste from breakrooms calls for thick liners such as the Berry Rhino-X 38x60 liners, a 17-micron high-density, leak-resistant bag in a 200-count case, which reduce the bag-failure cleanups that crews otherwise log as extra time. Multifold towels such as Pacific Blue Basic folded towels, sold in 4,000-towel cases of 16 packs, keep hand-drying costs predictable at the sink. A high-capacity cart such as the Rubbermaid Commercial janitorial cart, with a 34-gallon zippered bag, 8-inch wheels, and a locking door cabinet, lets one tech carry degreaser, descaler, and food-safe sanitizer securely, which matters when chemicals are staged near food areas.

faqs.q: Is breakroom cleaning normally included in a standard office cleaning contract?
faqs.a: Surface-level breakroom cleaning is usually included or priced as a $12–$25 per-visit add-on covering counters, sink, microwave, refrigerator exterior, and cabinet pulls. Deep tasks such as refrigerator purges, appliance degreasing, and brewer descaling are usually excluded unless the scope exhibit names them with a frequency.

faqs.q: How much extra does a breakroom deep sanitization work order usually cost?
faqs.a: Most vendors bill deep sanitization at specialty rates of $55–$95 per hour with a $90–$135 minimum per visit. A single-breakroom deep clean covering refrigerator purge, microwave and toaster-oven degreasing, and brewer descaling typically takes 1.5 to 3 hours, so expect roughly $135–$285 per event.

faqs.q: What safety documentation should a vendor provide for breakroom chemicals?
faqs.a: Under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, the vendor must keep Safety Data Sheets for every degreaser, descaler, and disinfectant and train staff on them. Ask for copies, confirm labeled secondary containers, and verify that disinfectants used on food-contact surfaces are followed by a food-safe sanitizer or rinse per label dwell time. Green Seal or EPA Safer Choice products are a reasonable requirement for occupied offices.

faqs.q: How do I convert a per-visit breakroom add-on into a monthly number?
faqs.a: Multiply visits per week by 4.33 to get visits per month, then multiply by the per-visit price. Five visits per week equals 21.65 visits, so a $18 add-on is about $390 per month. Use the same 4.33 factor to compare weekly deep tasks against monthly or quarterly pricing.

faqs.q: Should the vendor's certificate of insurance cover appliance damage?
faqs.a: Yes. Confirm the COI lists general liability and names your company or landlord as additional insured, and ask whether care, custody, and control exclusions would block a claim if a tech damages a refrigerator seal or a brewer during descaling. Specialty deep work is where those claims tend to arise.
